title: Sweeping a room
hook: a priest arrives filthy at the music, and his poem says who sweeps a room as for God makes it fine
tomorrow: why would a priest thank God for freckles?

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Collar: Herbert raging that he was done with God's service, until one word cut through the shouting. Child. And he answered, My Lord. Today, the same priest is out on a muddy road.

A broom may be the least holy-looking thing in a house. So can sweeping a floor be a prayer? Herbert has a line for that, and a story behind it. George Herbert, the country priest behind this week's poems, is walking to Salisbury for the music he loves: the cathedral, and a music meeting with friends after. On the road, a poor man's horse has fallen under its load. Herbert takes off his coat, helps unload the horse, gets it up, and loads it again. He arrives at the music late, and filthy.
screen: `A BROOM. A PRAYER?` → `A HORSE DOWN ON THE ROAD.` → `HERBERT TAKES OFF HIS COAT.` → `LATE, AND FILTHY.`

segments.voice: One of his friends said he'd lowered himself with such dirty work. Izaak Walton, who wrote Herbert's Life, says Herbert answered the thought of what he'd done would be music to him at midnight. That's the story. Here's the poem it lives in, The Elixir. It opens: "Teach me, my God and King, / In all things thee to see". Then the verse at its center: "A servant with this clause / Makes drudgery divine: / Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine." An elixir, in old alchemy, was the stuff that turned lead to gold. Herbert's elixir is the clause itself: for thy sake. The poem says nothing is so mean, so low, that it won't grow bright and clean when it's done for God. Herbert didn't invent this. It's an old Christian teaching about work, and Paul wrote it to the church at Colossae: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." It's why some Christians offer the day's work to God before they start it, and why these verses are still sung as a hymn. Notice what the poem doesn't promise. The broom doesn't get lighter. What changes is who the work is for. Herbert meant God. Some readers who don't pray hear the clause pointing at whoever walks into the clean room next.
screen: `MUSIC TO HIM AT MIDNIGHT.` · `THE ELIXIR: IN ALL THINGS THEE TO SEE.` · `DRUDGERY DIVINE.` · `AS TO THE LORD, NOT UNTO MEN.` · then, large: `SWEEPING AS PRAYER.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, sweep or wipe one small surface near you: a desk, a step, a corner of the counter. Go slowly, all the way into the edges. If you pray, you can say Herbert's clause under your breath, for thy sake; if not, keep in mind the person who'll use this space next.
Sweeping a room: Herbert's picture of the lowest chore made fine, because of who it's done for. In The Elixir, the clause is the gold.
Your line: sweeping as prayer. The fallen horse on the Salisbury road was the same poem, walked out. That's the last of Herbert for now.
